replying_to: Replying to NorMuon: Making Muon more efficient and scalable
display_title: Official Review of Submission23201 by Reviewer eCSL

summary.value: The paper proposes NorMuon, an optimizer that augments Muon with neuron-wise adaptive normalization to balance uneven update magnitudes after orthogonalization. It also introduces an efficient FSDP2-based distributed implementation. Experiments on models up to 5.4B parameters show faster convergence and higher efficiency than AdamW, Muon, and Dion, with minimal overhead.

strengths.value:
* The paper clearly identifies a real limitation of Muon (uneven neuron updates) and addresses it with a simple, elegant normalization scheme.
* The distributed FSDP2 implementation is well-designed, maintaining scalability with low communication cost.

weaknesses.value:
* NorMuon mainly combines Muon’s orthogonalization with Adam-mini–style normalization; the algorithmic change is minimal and lacks new theoretical insight.
* In Section 4.1.1, all model sizes are trained on the same number of tokens rather than following scaling-law-based (e.g., chinchilla law) token allocation.
* The distributed results are limited to 16 GPUs; communication efficiency and load balancing on 64–256 GPU clusters remain untested.
* The method’s robustness to $\beta_1$, $beta_2$ and learning rate scaling is not explored.

questions.value: * The paper only provides visualization from a single layer at one checkpoint in Figure 1; could the authors include additional visualizations across different layers or training stages for completeness?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission23201 by Reviewer eCSL

comment.value:
Thank you for your valuable comments. Please find our response to each of your concerns below:

-------

**W1. NorMuon mainly combines Muon’s orthogonalization with Adam-mini–style normalization; the algorithmic change is minimal and lacks new theoretical insight.**

We agree that the final NorMuon is a few-lines of code change, and we view this simplicity as an advantage. Our contribution lies in recognizing that strengths of Muon and Adam-like adaptive methods are complementary rather than conflicting. NorMuon combines their strengths with a *specific* form of variance adaptation with minimal overhead. Crucially, the design of NorMuon is not an arbitrary combination: we make several design choices—neuron-wise statistics, placement of adaptivity, parameters to apply—and support these choices with ablations. In addition, while Adam-like optimizers do not require distributed algorithmic considerations, Muon and NorMuon do. As part of this work, we design an efficient distributed version of NorMuon that improves praticality of both optimizers.

We also acknowledge that we do not provide a full theoretical convergence analysis. This is largely due to the complexity of modern LLMs, where analyzing end-to-end optimization behavior remains beyond the reach of current theoretical tools. This limitation is shared by many recent optimizer works, e.g. Muon and SOAP. They are motivated by second-order intuitions and empirical evidence rather than complete convergence guarantees. In the same spirit, our contribution is primarily empirical: we diagnose a deficiency in Muon’s neuron-level behavior and show that neuron-wise adaptive mechanism can effectively address it in practice.


------

**W2. In Section 4.1.1, all model sizes are trained on the same number of tokens rather than following scaling-law-based (e.g., chinchilla law) token allocation.**

Thanks for pointing this out. Our original experiments fixed the token budget to 50B for both 1.1B and 5.4B models due to resource constraints, even though Chinchilla-style scaling would ideally allocate more tokens to the larger model.

To address this, we have conducted additional experiments where the 1.1B and 5.4B models are trained under a 1× Chinchilla-style token allocation. The validation loss curves are provided [here](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/NorMuon_rebuttal-C3E8/Loss_curve_chinchilla/), and the table below reports the percentage reduction in training steps required for each optimizer to match Adam’s final validation loss under this setting:

| **Optimizer** | **1.1B** | **5.4B** |
| ----- | ---- | ---- |
| Muon          | 19.16%   | 5.6%     |
| NorMuon       | 25.04%   | 13.17%   |

NorMuon continues to achieve consistently lower validation loss than both AdamW and Muon, and it yields the best training efficiency under Chinchilla-style token allocation. We will include these results and experimental details in the revised version to better support our claims about efficiency across scaling-law–consistent setups.


------

**W3. The distributed results are limited to 16 GPUs; communication efficiency and load balancing on 64–256 GPU clusters remain untested.**

Clusters with 64–256 GPUs are unfortunately beyond our current resource budget, but we have extended our experiments from 16 to 32 GPUs to further stress-test our distributed implementation.

On 32 GPUs, we obtain the following timings:

| **model** | **Optimizer step time** | **Training step time** |
| ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| adam      | 0.016                   | 14.99                  |
| NorMuon   | 0.46                    | 15.43 (2.9%$\uparrow$) |

As shown in the table, under 32 GPUs, the total training step time is still under 3% increase. This is because (i) the forward and backward passes dominate wall-clock time, and (ii) with more GPUs, our distributed scheme parallelizes orthogonalization across devices, so the per-GPU optimizer cost shrinks.

At even larger scales (64–256 GPUs), one typically combines FSDP with additional forms of parallelism (tensor, pipeline, sequence, etc.), which would require further engineering and system design. We view these as valuable future directions. Our results on 32 GPUs show that NorMuon’s distributed design can keep the end-to-end step-time overhead small, and we believe this serves as a practical building block for scaling orthogonalization-based optimizers to larger clusters.


------

**Q1. The paper only provides visualization from a single layer at one checkpoint in Figure 1; could the authors include additional visualizations across different layers or training stages for completeness?**

Thanks for the suggestion. We provide more visualizations across different layers and training stages [here](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/NorMuon_rebuttal-C3E8/updates_visualization/). The early, mid and final stages correspond to 10B, 30B and 50B training tokens checkpoints.

summary.value: This work proposes NorMuon, applying row-wise normalization to muon after orthogonalization, to ensure balanced parameter utilization while preserving Muon’s conditioning benefits. The idea is reasonable, and the experiment demonstrates a potentially promising result.

strengths.value:
1. The motivation is reasonable.
2. The optimizer design and implementation have considered memory and distributed optimization, which is good for practical applications.

weaknesses.value: 1. There are several points to clarify further, including whether there is implicit LR tuning bias and some details. See questions.

questions.value:
1. Could the authors further ensure there is no implicit LR tuning bias? As the 0.2 in line 10 of the algorithm is likely an empirical value, how much effort does it cost to get this value? This actually affects the effective learning rate.
    What's more, the Beta value is also different from Adam/Muon. The Beta tuning is also a source of implicit LR tuning bias. How much tuning does it take, or is there a theoretical explanation for the value? What if the authors put the same tuning effort into Muon? Would NorMuon still be superior?

2. The authors say, "we apply orthogonalization to the concatenated QKV matrix rather than separately for a fair comparison". Then how are those matrices concatenated? As NorMuon is using row-wise normalization, this detail should be provided.

3. With lines 9 and 10 in Algorithm 1, there would be a double scaling. Isn't $ \sqrt{mn} /  ||\widehat{O_t}||_F$ very close to 1? (It feels like the difference is only caused by epsilon.) For "match Adam’s RMS norm", it is row-wise or matrix-wise?

Thanks for your insightful questions. Please see our response per each of your concerns below:

------

**Q1. Could the authors further ensure there is no implicit LR tuning bias? As the 0.2 in line 10 of the algorithm is likely an empirical value, how much effort does it cost to get this value? This actually affects the effective learning rate. What's more, the Beta value is also different from Adam/Muon. The Beta tuning is also a source of implicit LR tuning bias. How much tuning does it take, or is there a theoretical explanation for the value? What if the authors put the same tuning effort into Muon? Would NorMuon still be superior?**

Thanks for pointing this out and we agree that hyperparameters are very important. The 0.2 in Algorithm 1 is an empirical value following [1], and we use the same value for Muon. To address your concern on tuning bias, below we clarify (i) how hyperparameters were chosen in the original experiments and (ii) additional tuning we performed to validate robustness.

**(i) Original setup**

In the main experiments on 1.1B/5.4B models:

- For Adam, we directly adopt the hyperparameters from Tinyllama and tune the learning rate.
- For Muon, we further tune the learning rate while keeping other hyperparameters (except $\beta_1$ in Muon) unchanged. We use the default $\beta_1$ suggested by Muon blog.
- For NorMuon, we keep the same hyperparameters as Muon to ensure there is no tuning bias toward NorMuon.

In the experiments on 124M and 350M models, we adopt the already highly tuned hyperparameters on modded-nanogpt leaderboard for Muon. And we conduct further tuning of $\beta_1$ for NorMuon.

**(ii) Additional Tuning**

To make the comparison more rigorous, we performed further hyperparameter sweeps on the 1.1B model trained on 1×Chinchilla tokens (20B, for efficiency) for all methods, covering learning rate, $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$ and weight decay.

The main results are summarized below, with the first line being the currently used config. The best two results are in bold. Note that for Muon/NorMuon, we tune the learning rate ratio in Algorithm 1 instead of learning rate following [1].

|| -| -| -| 0.2| **2.174**|

| ------------- | ----------------------- | ------------- | ---------------- | ------------------- |
| Muon| 0.2| 0.95| 0.1| **2.134**|
|| 0.1| -| -| 2.154|
|| 0.4| -| -| **2.135**|
|| -| 0.9| -| 2.175|

| ------------- | ---- | --- | ---- | ---------------- | ------------------- |
| NorMuon       | 0.2 | 0.95          | 0.95          | 0.1              | **2.128**           |

As shown, further tuning yields minimal improvement on validation loss, indicating that our original configurations were already well-tuned. And this can support that NorMuon is still superior than Muon under with the same amount of tuning.



------

**Q2. The authors say, "we apply orthogonalization to the concatenated QKV matrix rather than separately for a fair comparison". Then how are those matrices concatenated? As NorMuon is using row-wise normalization, this detail should be provided.**

Thank you for pointing this out. We concatenate Q, K, V **along the output dimension**. For $Q \in W^{d\times d_q}, K \in W^{d\times d_k}, V \in W^{d\times d_v}$, we concat them to $W_{qkv} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times (d_q+d_k+d_v)}$.

Orthogonalization and NorMuon’s neuron-wise normalization are then applied to this concatenated matrix.

In Algorithm 1, we use meancols because PyTorch typically stores weight matrices in a transposed layout (so the tensor we operate on is effectively $W_{qkv}^T$). Thus, meancols will results in statistics of shape $\mathbb{R}^{(d_q+d_k+d_v)}$. We will make this dimension convention and the concatenation detail explicit in the revision to avoid confusion.

comment.value:
**Q3. With lines 9 and 10 in Algorithm 1, there would be a double scaling. Isn't very close to 1? (It feels like the difference is only caused by epsilon.) For "match Adam’s RMS norm", it is row-wise or matrix-wise?**

Lines 9 and 10 perform two different types of scaling:

* Line 9 is row-wise (per-neuron) scaling. Here we rescale each row/neuron using its own RMS statistic. This adjusts the relative update magnitudes across neurons. Some of the scaled neuron norm might not be close to one due to the EMA used for the statistics.

* Line 10 is matrix-wise scaling. After row-wise normalization, we apply a single global scalar to the entire matrix so that the overall RMS of NorMuon/Muon updates matches that of Adam. This preserves the relative scaling across neurons introduced by line 9, and only adjusts the global scale of the update. This step is mainly for ease of tuning: it allows us to reuse Adam’s learning rate schedule by matching Adam’s matrix-wise RMS norm, as recommended in [1].

### Reference

[1] Muon is Scalable for LLM Training

summary.value: This paper proposes NorMuon, an optimizer that augments Muon’s matrix-level orthogonalized updates with neuron-wise adaptive scaling via an EMA of per-row squared update norms, applied after orthogonalization and followed by an RMS re-scaling of the step size. The method aims to preserve Muon’s improved conditioning while reducing variance across neuron update magnitudes. A distributed FSDP2 implementation is described that assigns orthogonalization work across ranks and performs shard-local row normalization. Experiments on 1.1B and 5.4B-parameter LLM pretraining (50B tokens) and on Modded-NanoGPT (124M/350M) report faster convergence than AdamW, Muon, and Dion, with small wall-clock overhead and modest memory cost. The idea is simple and practically appealing; however, novelty over Muon + blockwise adaptivity is incremental, and several design choices (e.g., post-orthogonalization scaling) and evaluation details need tighter justification.

strengths.value:
- Clear diagnosis and motivation: figures show Muon improves conditioning but leaves high variance in per-neuron update norms; NorMuon directly targets this gap with a lightweight row-wise statistic and normalization.
- Simple, scalable design: the added state is $v_t\in\mathbb{R}^m$ (per row), keeping memory close to Muon; the distributed algorithm avoids fully replicated orthogonalization and keeps step-time overhead small in reported runs.
- Breadth of experiments and ablations: results at multiple scales (124M→5.4B), efficiency curves vs AdamW/Muon/Dion, and ablations on (i) coordinate- vs neuron-level adaptation (Muon+Adam), (ii) normalization before vs after orthogonalization, and (iii) restricting to $m>n$ matrices.

weaknesses.value:
- Limited novelty/positioning: the method is essentially “Muon + blockwise RMS adaptivity after orthogonalization,” which is close in spirit to Adam-mini/Adafactor-style reductions and concurrent Adamuon; theoretical justification is light beyond qualitative diagnostics.
- Evaluation fairness and metrics: efficiency is primarily reported as “% fewer steps to reach Adam’s final loss,” with different base LRs/betas/weight-decay policies across optimizers; the paper lacks hyperparameter sweeps per baseline, robustness/stability metrics, and downstream evaluations beyond validation loss at equal tokens.
- Distributed section clarity: Algorithm 2 elides details on communication overlap, determinism, and failure cases; the claimed 33–50% extra communication but ~3% step-time increase needs per-layer profiling, and the approach seems tied to row-wise sharding (how general is this across FSDP configs?).

questions.value:
- About the post-orthogonalization scaling: Eq. (10) uses $\hat{\eta}=0.2\,\eta\sqrt{mn}/\lVert\hat{O}_t\rVert_F$. Why $0.2$? Is this analytically derived from RMS-matching to Adam or tuned empirically? Please provide sensitivity curves and failure modes when varying this constant.
- About the second-moment estimator: in Eq. (7) $v_t=\beta_2 v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)\mathrm{meancols}(O_t\odot O_t)$, do you apply bias-correction (e.g., $\hat v_t$) in early steps? If not, why is it unnecessary here? Also clarify whether “meancols” (per-row mean over columns) is used for all 2D tensors, and list precisely which parameter classes (QKV concat, MLP up/down, embeddings, layer norms, biases) receive NorMuon vs a fallback optimizer.

We will include these results in our revision to better support our claim. To further prove the effectiveness of NorMuon, we also add a setting of supervised fine-tuning. Please refer to our response to Reviewer Ratf W3.


--------

**W3. Distributed section clarity: Algorithm 2 elides details on communication overlap, determinism, and failure cases; the claimed 33–50% extra communication but ~3% step-time increase needs per-layer profiling, and the approach seems tied to row-wise sharding (how general is this across FSDP configs?).**

Thank you for pointing out these missing details. We clarify below and will update Section 3.2 accordingly.

*Communication overlap and step-time overhead.* We ommit the details of communication overlap in Algorithm 2 because we see it as an implementation optimization, rather than a conceptual change to the algorithm. We provide more details here: Muon and NorMuon require the full weight matrix on a single GPU to perform orthogonalization, which require a gather step for sharded parameters. We overlap this gather with the orthogonalization compute. More specifically, we group parameters and:

1. launch an asynchronous gather for group 1;
2. once group 1 is ready, launch the gather for group 2 while performing orthogonalization on group 1;
3. iterate this process over all groups.

This pipeline hides much of the communication latency behind compute and helps explain why the optimizer step adds only about 3% to the total step time.

A second reason for the small overhead is that, in our training, forward+backward passes dominate wall-clock time. As reported in Table 2, the optimizer step accounts for <3% of the total step time, and within this, the orthogonalization compute is the dominant component. With NVLink and high-bandwidth interconnects, the incremental communication cost is relatively minor even without overlap.

For Determinism and Failure case: In our implementation, all gathers and orthogonalization calls are issued in a fixed per-layer order on each step, so NorMuon does not introduce extra nondeterminism relative to Muon+FSDP. We did not observe numerical or convergence failures, and the overhead stayed under 3%.

comment.value:
*Generality across FSDP sharding configurations.* NorMuon is not tied to a particular sharding scheme:

- When using row-wise sharding of weight matrices, NorMuon can fully leverage it with no additional communication beyond what Muon already requires, since we can keep and update the second-moment state on the GPU that performs orthogonalization.
- Under FSDP1-style flattening and chunk sharding, both Muon and NorMuon benefit from reduced communication: we only need to gather parameters that are actually sharded across GPUs, not all parameters. NorMuon still does **not** introduce any extra communication beyond Muon in this setting.
- For more general mixed sharding (e.g., combined row-wise and column-wise schemes), NorMuon can still be applied by aggregating per-row statistics via a lightweight all-reduce and then applying the same row-wise normalization. The additional communication over Muon is extremely small, since it operates only on per-row scalars (<1% of full parameter size). For optimal distributed Muon design under complex sharding, we view them as valuable future directions, and we believe this work serves as a practical building block for scaling orthogonalization-based optimizers to larger clusters.

We will expand the distributed section to explicitly describe these cases.


------

**Q1. About the post-orthogonalization scaling. Why 0.2? Is this analytically derived from RMS-matching to Adam or tuned empirically? Please provide sensitivity curves and failure modes when varying this constant.**

This scaling factor effectively controls the learning-rate for Muon/NorMuon. The specific value (0.2) is chosen **empirically** to approximately match the RMS of Adam’s updates, following the recommendation in [1].

In our tuning experiments (see W2 above), the learning-rate ratio yields smooth changes in validation loss rather than abrupt failures:

- Smaller ratios lead to slower convergence but stable training.
- Larger ratios improve convergence up to a point, after which training can become unstable (>=0.8), as is typical when increasing the effective learning rate too much.


------

**Q2. About the second-moment estimator: in Eq. (7) , do you apply bias-correction (e.g., ) in early steps? If not, why is it unnecessary here? Also clarify whether “meancols” (per-row mean over columns) is used for all 2D tensors, and list precisely which parameter classes (QKV concat, MLP up/down, embeddings, layer norms, biases) receive NorMuon vs a fallback optimizer.**

We do not apply bias correction to the second-moment estimator in NorMuon. The reason is that we subsequently perform RMS normalization of the update (line 10 in Algorithm 1), which rescales the per-neuron update to a target norm. Hence the bias-correction term will be canceled out.

We follow the Muon setting [2] and apply Muon/NorMuon to all 2D weight matrices in the hidden layers, including: attention projections (QKV and output projections), MLP up/down projections. For embeddings, layer norms, biases, and the lm head, we use AdamW, as is standard in Muon-style setups. Mean cols is applied to all parameters optimized by NorMuon.

------


### Reference

comment.value:
Thank you for the thoughtful follow-up and for engaging with our additional experiments! We appreciate the opportunity to clarify the performance comparison and distributed implementation.

---
>**Performance comparison with Muon**: From the hyperparameter sweeps, the validation losses of the two optimizers are very close. A simple Welch t-test gives a p-value around 0.24, I do not see strong statistical evidence. It is also hard to separate genuine optimizer gains from the effect of trying slightly more configurations for NorMuon.

We agree that the absolute differences in this short-run configuration are small. However, we would like to clarify why this does not undermine our conclusion that NorMuon meaningfully outperforms Muon.

**(a) Small absolute differences do not imply insignificant gains**

The magnitude of the validation-loss gap should be interpreted in the context of LLM training. Even small differences correspond to hundreds of optimizer steps on a 1.1B model. As shown in Appendix A.2:

* NorMuon reaches Adam’s final validation loss 5.88% faster than Muon.
* If we look at the Muon's final validation loss, NorMuon achieves the same loss 8.33% faster than Muon.

We believe these improvements in training efficiency are meaningful and practically significant.

**(b) Larger-budget and downstream results show a clearer separation**

The stronger evidence comes from longer training runs and downstream evaluation:

* Table 1 uses a longer training budget and shows **>10%** efficiency improvement for 1.1B model.
* Section 4.1.3 reports downstream benchmark results where NorMuon outperforms Muon on most tasks at both 1.1B and 5.4B scales, including notable improvements on OpenbookQA, Hellaswag and Winogrande.

**(c) The Welch t-test is not statistically valid for hyperparameter sweeps**

As the comment also noted, each sweep point corresponds to a different hyperparameter configuration, not repeated measurements under identical conditions. Thus, the i.i.d. assumption for the Welch t-test is violated. The sweep should be interpreted as a robustness check, not a statistical test.

What the sweep *does* show is:

* Across a broad range of LR / LR-ratio / betas / WD settings, NorMuon consistently outperforms Muon in all configuration we tested.
* The two additional $\beta_2$ configurations for NorMuon were included because hyperparameter sweeps across optimizers are requested; they are **not** the reason NorMuon performs better. In fact, excluding these $\beta_2$-tuned points, NorMuon still outperforms Muon.
* In our main experiments, we **do not** tune $\beta_2$ for NorMuon to avoid tuning bias; we use the same settings for other hyperparameters as Muon.

Therefore, we respectfully disagree with the interpretation that “it is hard to separate genuine optimizer gains from slightly more configurations for NorMuon.” The gains persist under strictly matched hyperparameters.

Finally, regarding significance: validation loss is a stable metric with low variance across random data orders, and prior work [1,2] typically reports single run for each configuration. A statistically meaningful Welch t-test would require multiple repeated runs for each optimizer, which would exceed 900 GPU hours (3 runs per optimizer)—far beyond the scope of typical evaluations.

Overall, all evidence—robustness sweeps, full-budget runs, and downstream tasks—indicates that NorMuon consistently and notably outperforms Muon, and these gains are not a consequence of extra tuning.


>**Communication overlap and step-time overhead**

Your understanding is correct: there is no overlap within a single matrix, and the overlap arises entirely from pipelining across parameter groups.

As requested, we have added a timeline visualization (Appendix D) illustrating this pipelined schedule using a simple example with 2 GPUs and 3 parameter groups. This pattern naturally generalizes to more GPUs and more groups.

Regarding the <3% step-time overhead: this number reflects both our implementation techniques (orthogonalization distribution and communication overlap) and the dominance of the forward/backward passes.

To disentangle the contributions:

* As shown in Table 3, without orthogonalization distribution, the optimizer-step time increases from 0.84s to 2.29s, yielding an 8% overhead.
* We further profile an implementation without communication overlap and it yields a 4.5% overhead.
* Combining orthogonalization distribution and communication overlap reduces the overhead to <3%, making it negligible relative to the forward/backward pass.

Both techniques are therefore necessary to achieve the reported efficiency.

---
**Minor comments**

We have corrected the typos you pointed out. Thank you for flagging them!

---
[1] SOAP: Improving and Stabilizing Shampoo Using Adam
[2] Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them

Please let us know if there are any additional questions or concerns - we are happy to provide further clarification.

summary.value: This paper introduces NorMuon, an optimizer that improves upon the recently proposed Muon optimizer for training large language models. The authors identify that while Muon effectively reduces condition numbers through orthogonalization, it produces highly non-uniform per-neuron update norms that cause imbalanced optimization. NorMuon addresses this by adding neuron-wise adaptive learning rates through lightweight second-order momentum statistics and row-wise normalization applied after orthogonalization. The authors develop an efficient distributed implementation that minimizes computational overhead while strategically distributing orthogonalization across devices.

strengths.value:
1. The paper proposed a simple yet effective Solution. NorMuon's design is elegantly simple, adding neuron-wise normalization after orthogonalization, and making it easy to understand and implement. 

2. Comprehensive experimental validation. The experimental evaluation is thorough and convincing, such as multiple scales tested (124M, 350M, 1.1B, 5.4B parameters), consistent improvements across all scales, comparisons against strong baselines (Adam, Muon, Dion). 

3. Rigorous ablation studies. The ablation experiments (Section 4.1.3 and Appendix A.1) systematically validate design choices: Neuron-wise vs. coordinate-wise adaptive rates, Normalization positioning (before vs. after orthogonalization).

weaknesses.value:
1. Limited Scope of Experiments: No downstream task evaluation. All results are pretraining validation loss; no evaluation on actual downstream tasks. 

2. Limited Scope of Experiments: Single dataset per scale. 1.1B/5.4B models only tested on SlimPajama; 124M/350M only on FineWeb. 

3. I think validation loss is not a great metric for LLM training. A smaller validation loss usually does not mean a better performance. The authors can provide the performance of downstream tasks and the performance of fine-tuning or RL fine-tuning tasks. 

4. The motivation is not very clear to me. I'm not very clear why a more uniform per-neuron norm can achieve a better performance.

Thanks for your valuable comments! Let us address your concerns as follows:

------

**W1. Limited Scope of Experiments: No downstream task evaluation. All results are pretraining validation loss; no evaluation on actual downstream tasks.**

Thank you for raising this important point. To address it, we evaluated the pretrained 1.1B and 5.4B models on a suite of pretraining benchmarks: OpenBookQA, HellaSwag, ARC-Easy, WSC273, Winogrande, BoolQ, and PIQA.

The results are shown below

*1.1B model*

| **Optimizer** | **Avg**     | **OpenBookQA** | **Hellaswag** | **Arc-E** | **WSC273** | **Winograde** | **BoolQ** | **PIQA**  |
| ------------- | ----------- | -------------- | ------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------- | --------- | --------- |
| AdamW         | 53.80 | 31             | 47.35         | 53.45     | 62.64      | 53.12         | 59.14     | 69.91     |
| Muon          | 53.91 | 31.6           | 48.12         | 55.22     | 58.24      | 52.57         | **60.76** | 70.89     |
| NorMuon       | **55.34** | **33.4**       | **48.7**      | **55.85** | **65.57**  | **53.43**     | 59.51     | **70.95** |

*5.4B model*

| **model** | **Avg** | **OpenBookQA** | **Hellaswag** | **Arc-E** | **WSC273** | **Winograde** | **BoolQ** | **PIQA**  |
| --------- | ------- | -------------- | ------------- | --------- | ---------- | ------------- | --------- | --------- |
| adam      | 60.59   | 35.6           | 59.98         | 62.79     | **72.16**  | 58.48         | 61.62     | 73.5      |
| Muon      | 60.65   | 35.4           | 59.99         | 63.51     | 72.1       | 58.33         | 60.73     | 74.48     |
| NorMuon   | **61.74**   | **36.4**       | **61.35**     | **63.93** | **72.16**  | **60.3**      | **63.46** | **74.59** |

Across both model sizes, NorMuon achieves the best average downstream performance and is the best on almost all tasks, which also correlates with the validation loss. We will include these results in our revision to better support our claim.

------

**W2. Limited Scope of Experiments: Single dataset per scale. 1.1B/5.4B models only tested on SlimPajama; 124M/350M only on FineWeb.**

We agree that testing on more datasets can strengthen the empirical claims. However, training and tuning 1.1B/5.4B models on additional large-scale corpora would require substantial compute which is beyond our resource budget. To still provide evidence of generality, we added new experiments at the 124M and 350M scales on the C4 dataset, and re-tuned Muon and NorMuon for this setting.

We include the validation loss curve under this [link](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/NorMuon_rebuttal-C3E8/Loss_curve_C4/).

For both model sizes, we observe that NorMuon consistently attains lower validation loss than Muon throughout training. When we extend Muon’s training to match NorMuon’s final loss, Muon needs ≈6% more steps to reach the same validation loss. These results also align with the results on the Fineweb dataset.

------

**W3. I think validation loss is not a great metric for LLM training. A smaller validation loss usually does not mean a better performance. The authors can provide the performance of downstream tasks and the performance of fine-tuning or RL fine-tuning tasks.**

For downstream pretraining evaluation, please see our response to W1 where we evaluate 1.1B and 5.4B pretrained models on pretraining benchmarks.

To further prove the effectiveness of NorMuon, we add a setting of supervised fine-tuning. We conduct long-reasoning math SFT using Qwen 2.5 Math 7B as the initial model. We fine-tune on the open-r1/Mixture-of-Thoughts dataset for 87k prompts (covering mathematics and science) and evaluate on MATH 500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and GPQA.

| **Optimizer** | **Avg**   | **MATH 500** | **AIME24** | **AIME25** | **GPQA**  |
| ------------- | --------- | ------------ | ---------- | ---------- | --------- |
| AdamW         | 43.36     | 80.6         | 25.73      | 23.96      | **43.18** |
| Muon          | 43.58     | 81.2         | **27.5**   | 23.49      | 42.11     |
| NorMuon       | **44.02** | **82.2**     | 26.6       | **24.69**  | 42.61     |

As shown, NorMuon achieves the best average performance. This shows that NorMuon can still be effective under SFT setting. We would also like to note that previous work [1] demonstrates that the alignment of optimizers used in pretraining and SFT can affect the performance. Hence, the improvement of NorMuon could be more significant if it's applied on LLMs pretrained by Muon-like optimizer.

**W4. The motivation is not very clear to me. I'm not very clear why a more uniform per-neuron norm can achieve a better performance.**

Our motivation began with the question: Is Muon a direct replacement for Adam, or can the strengths of the two approaches be combined? Through analysis of update dynamics, we observed that Muon produces high variance in per-neuron update norms: a small subset of neurons effectively sees much larger step sizes, while many others receive much smaller updates.

Then we propose NorMuon to address this by applying an adaptive learning rate at the neuron level, so that each neuron’s effective step size is better aligned, while keeping Muon’s well-conditioned updates at the matrix level.

This follows the same principle as adaptive methods such as Adam and Adam-mini, which can be interpreted as enforcing similar signal-to-noise ratios across coordinates or parameter blocks. By reducing the variance of per-neuron update norms, one can prevent a few neurons from dominating learning, and avoids others being effectively “frozen” due to small updates.

-----

**Q1. In my opinion, optimizer is very sensitive to the selection of hyperparameters, I would like to ask whether the authors fully tuned the hyperparameters of the baseline methods.**

We agree that the selection of hyperparameters is very important. Below we clarify (i) how hyperparameters were chosen in the original experiments and (ii) additional tuning we performed to validate robustness.

**(i) Original setup**

In the main experiments on 1.1B/5.4B models:

- For Adam, we directly adopt the hyperparameters from Tinyllama and tune the learning rate.
- For Muon, we further tune the learning rate while keeping other hyperparameters (except $\beta_1$ in Muon) unchanged. We use the default $\beta_1$ suggested by Muon blog.
- For NorMuon, we keep the same hyperparameters as Muon to avoid any tuning bias.

In the experiments on 124M and 350M models, we adopt the already highly tuned hyperparameters on modded-nanogpt leaderboard for Muon. And we conduct further tuning of $\beta_1$ for NorMuon.

**Additional Tuning**

To make the comparison more rigorous, we performed further hyperparameter sweeps on the 1.1B model trained on 1×Chinchilla tokens (20B, for efficiency) for all methods, covering learning rate, $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$ and weight decay.

summary.value:
The work proposes a new optimizer NorMuon which augments Muon with neuron-level adaptive normalization to balance update magnitudes after orthogonalization. It also provides an efficient FSDP2-based distributed implementation and experiments on models up to 5.4B parameters show faster convergence and higher efficiency than competing baselines such as AdamW, Muon and Dion with minimal overhead.

Reviewers raised number of concerns and comments, including:

Limited scope of experiments:
- No downstream task evaluations beyond validation loss
- Use of a single dataset per scale
- Lack of robustness and stability analyses with respect to hyperparameters, including the learning rate
- Token counts not adjusted consistently across different scales
- Limited distributed results beyond 16 GPUs for justifing communication efficiency and load balancing

Unclear motivation and intuition: While the motivation to balance per-neuron update magnitudes is intuitive, it remains unclear why enforcing more uniform per-neuron norms should lead to improved performance.

Limited algorithmic novelty and lack of new theoretical insight.

In addition, the reviewers raised several concerns regarding the clarity of presentation and experimental setup.

reviewer_concerns.value:
The authors responded to all concerns by providing additional empirical evidence and clarifications. However, many of the concerns appear to be only partially addressed, and a more systematic approach is needed to fully resolve the issues related to experimental validation, including statistical significance, experimental scope, and fairness of the comparisons.

While the algorithmic advancement over existing optimizers appears limited, the paper would benefit from stronger and clearer justification for why a uniform balancing approach should lead to improved performance. Providing either more compelling empirical evidence or new theoretical insights in this direction would significantly strengthen the contribution.

reviewer_scores.value:
Given the breadth of comments, it is difficult to predict how the scores would change. There were several concerns, missing ablations, and issues related to clarity and presentation, and a thorough discussion might have influenced some reviewers to increase their scores and potentially push the paper over the borderline. However, I believe the paper still requires too many improvements. As a result, unfortunately, I am leaning toward recommending rejection.

That said, there were many constructive suggestions aimed at improving the presentation and strengthening the results, and I hope the authors will take advantage of these suggestions regardless of the final decision.
